1:
The word rendered congregation is the first difficulty. Charles Ellicott says the rendering comes of a mistaken derivation: as pointed, the Hebrew must mean silence. Of the many conjectures he would choose between a word for gods, applied to judges as at Psalm 82:6, and a particle meaning but; and if the first is preferred, as most modern scholars prefer it, sons of men becomes accusative — do ye judge the sons of men with equity? John Gill reports that the word signifies a sheaf, to which a bench of judges may be compared, but that Jarchi and R. Moses take it of dumbness — do ye indeed speak dumb justice — which would make the verse an accusation of criminal silence. John Calvin rejects one solution because it breaks the parallelism, which requires will ye speak righteousness to answer will ye judge uprightness.

Who is addressed most of them agree, and one dissents. Matthew Henry takes them for a bench of justices brought up in statutes so righteous that no other nation’s were comparable; one would not have thought such men could be bribed, and yet they were, because the son of Kish could do for them what the son of Jesse could not 1 Samuel 22:7. Adam Clarke follows Bishop Patrick, that Saul, missing David, called a council which adjudged him guilty of treason. John Wesley names Saul’s judges, and notes that sons of men reminds them that they must give account to God. Keil and Delitzsch dissent: the psalm belongs to the time of Absalom, and its incomparable boldness does not warrant denying it to David, since in no one psalm do we meet so many high-flown figures within so narrow a compass.

John Calvin reads the opening as a challenge showing conscious rectitude: the justice of a cause is demonstratively evident when we appeal to the opposite party himself, and David repels by a declaration forced from their own lips the charges with which they had blackened him. C.H. Spurgeon turns on the numbers instead. Because the band unanimously condemned him they took their verdict for a right one; but what everybody says must be true is a lying proverb, resting on the presumption of large combinations. Some around Saul were passive rather than active persecutors, and the first sentence asks them to justify their silence: silence gives consent, and he who refrains from defending the right is an accomplice in the wrong.

The second verse is read as a picture of the scales. Adam Clarke makes it explicit: with their tongues they gave evil counsel, in their hearts they meditated nothing but wickedness, and though they held the scales of justice they made them balances of injustice — Justice with her balances being the emblem of the court but not of its practice. Charles Ellicott notes the antithesis between heart and land, the mischief conceived in the heart being weighed out instead of justice. John Wesley adds that they did great wrong under pretence of justice while they turned the scale. John Gill takes it of the manner: sinning not through surprise but with premeditation, and persisting in it.

Augustine of Hippo hears the verse addressed to all mankind by Truth itself. To what unjust man is it not easy to speak justice, he asks, or who, questioned about justice when he has no cause at stake, would not easily answer what is just? For the hand of our Maker has written this truth in our very hearts: what you would not have done to yourself, do not do to another. Of this no one was suffered to be ignorant even before the Law was given, so that there might be a rule by which to judge those who had no Law; and lest men complain that something was wanting, it was written on tables which in their hearts they would not read.
3:
Adam Clarke opens with a structural proposal no one else makes. Dr Kennicott, he reports, took this verse and the two following for the answer of Jehovah to the question of the first two, verses six to eight for the answer of the psalmist, and the remainder for the decree of Jehovah. On that reading the description of men always wicked, brought up in falsehood and lying, comes from God.

How early the estrangement begins they answer two ways. John Gill makes it the original corruption of nature, which accounts for all the wickedness done by men: they are conceived in sin and transgressors from the womb, alienated from God and from the godly life he requires. John Wesley says the same shortly — their natures are corrupt from birth, and they go astray by actual sins as soon as ever they are capable of reason. Charles Ellicott reasons in the opposite direction: the poet passes from his challenge to the unjust judges to speak of the wicked generally, and finds that such maturity of vice points to very early depravity, since hardened sinners of this kind must have been cradled in wickedness.

The serpent then holds the ground. Charles Ellicott observes that the figure is heightened, since the animal is supposed to have been first tamed and then suddenly darts forth its fangs, showing itself not only untamed but untameable; the adder he identifies with the Egyptian cobra, the species on which the charmers practise. John Gill allows three senses of the poison: their wrath against God and his people, their devouring words, or the malignity of sin in them, which like a serpent’s venom lies latent, infects every faculty and is incurable without the grace of God. Adam Clarke presses the figure into slander. As the poison of a bite is carried into the blood and circulates through the system carrying death everywhere, so injurious speeches circulate through society and blast a reputation in every place; against such there is no defence but God.

Whether serpent charming is a real art divides them further. Adam Clarke calls it an indisputable fact that in ancient times there were persons who charmed serpents, citing Ecclesiastes 10:11 and Jeremiah 8:17 with Virgil on the cold snake burst in the meadows by incantation. He supposes a species of adder nearly deaf, whose instinct warns it that listening would make it a prey. John Wesley reports that the Arabic writers name certain serpents which they call deaf — not because they are dull of hearing, as one of them expressly says, but because they will not be charmed. John Gill is more sceptical. He gathers the classical testimony from Pliny, Lucan, Virgil and Horace, that serpents have been drawn from their holes or burst asunder by muttered words; but the asp, he says, is unmoved by enchantments, and the psalmist neither approves of them nor affirms their virtue to be real — he takes his similitude only from the seeming deafness of serpents, to set forth the obstinacy of wicked men.

Two illustrations close the passage. Charles Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word for charmers is formed from the sound the charmer makes in imitating the snake, and quotes Lane’s description of an Egyptian charmer who assumes an air of mystery, strikes the walls with a palm stick and makes a clacking noise with his tongue; charming never so wisely is literally one tying knots wisely. The deaf adder, he adds, was a favourite image with Shakespeare, no doubt derived from this psalm. Adam Clarke gives instead a passage of the Old Psalter, where the snake fastens one ear to the earth and stops the other with her tail so as not to be brought to light — and so, it says, do the wicked, who stop their ears with love of earthly things, that they may not hear the voice of Christ.
6:
Matthew Henry begins by clearing the prayer of a charge. David prays against his enemies as enemies of God’s church and people, so that he was actuated by a public spirit and not by private revenge. He then notices what is not asked. David does not say, break their necks — no, let them live to repent, slay them not, lest my people forget — but break their teeth, for they are young lions that live by rapine; and the point is not that they should not feed themselves but that they should not make prey of others.

What the teeth stand for they answer variously. John Gill takes them for malicious words, calumnies and detractions, teeth being the instrument of speech, so that breaking them means preventing the mischief designed; God can take away the power and instruments of hurting, smiting his enemies on the cheekbone. Adam Clarke keeps Saul and his courtiers in view as lions, whose power of mischief is greatly lessened if their teeth are broken, but allows that the serpents of the previous verse may be meant, the prayer then being to destroy the fangs in which the poison is contained — save me from the adders, the sly and poisonous slanderers, and from the lions. C.H. Spurgeon puts the same request in the charmer’s terms: if they have no capacity for good, at least deprive them of their ability for evil, and treat them as the snake-charmers treat their serpents, extracting the fangs. A second beast is fetched in, he observes, as though one had not evil enough in it: the wicked are likened to young lions, monsters in the prime of their vigour, whose grinders are to be dashed out that they may be harmless. Charles Ellicott marks the transition as abrupt, from an obstinacy deaf to all charms to a violence that must be tamed by force, and renders great teeth literally as biters, or grinders. John Wesley calls them their instruments of doing mischief.

The melting waters of the next verse draw four pictures. Matthew Henry takes them for the waters of a land-flood, which though formidable for a while soon soak into the ground, or else for water spilt upon the ground, which cannot be gathered up but gradually dries away; such, he says, shall the floods of ungodly men be which sometimes make us afraid. Adam Clarke makes them desert waters, soon evaporated or absorbed by the sand. John Wesley makes them waters from melted snow, which run at first with great force but are suddenly gone. C.H. Spurgeon offers mountain torrents dried up by summer heats, or water spilt which none can find again — be gone, ye foul streams, he says, the sooner forgotten the better for the universe.

John Gill canvasses the versions rather than the images. The clause may mean let them be disheartened; or let them be unstable as water continually running; or let them come to nought, as the Greek and Latin have it; or let them be despised, as Jarchi and the Syriac read it, water being useless once it is past; or let their ruin be as swift as gliding water and as irrecoverable.

The bow of the same verse is ambiguous, and Adam Clarke says so. On one reading it is the adversaries who aim their envenomed shafts, and the prayer is that their arrows may not only fall short but be broken to pieces in the flight; but some apply the clause to God, and then when he bends his bow they shall be exterminated. Matthew Henry takes the first way, that the enemy’s arrows may fall at his feet and never come near the mark. C.H. Spurgeon takes the second, that when the Lord goes forth to war his judgments may so tell upon these persecutors that they be utterly cut in pieces.
8:
The snail is explained from its own habits. John Gill says that when it comes out of its shell it liquefies, drops its moisture and with that makes a path, from which it has its Hebrew name; the Targum reads the verse so. Adam Clarke gives the Chaldee at length — they shall melt away in their sins as water flows off, as the creeping snail that smears its track, as the untimely birth and the blind mole, which do not see the sun — and offers two derivations of the Hebrew word. It may come from the word for a path, because the creature leaves a shining track by emitting a portion of slime, and might therefore be called the pathmaker; or from words meaning to dwell in a winding spiral shell, which it carries with it wherever it goes. John Wesley reduces the whole to three words: quickly dissolved.

The verse about the pots and the thorns is another matter, and Charles Ellicott says plainly that it defeats him. The figure is generally intelligible, and like the images before it must convey abortive effort and sudden ruin; some experience of eastern travel undoubtedly supplied it, though accident or a copyist’s error has rendered it obscure. But the text as it stands resists all attempts to translate it. Literally the Hebrew runs, before shall understand your pots a bramble, as living, as heat sweeps them off. The ancient versions mostly render thorns instead of pots and make the simile the destruction of the bush before it grows to maturity, though he thinks the English versions have caught the figure better. His objection is that the Hebrew verb rendered feel could hardly be used of inanimate objects: even if a kettle might be said to feel the fire, we should hardly speak of its feeling the fuel. Some change in the text must therefore be made, and a very slight change in one letter gives excellent sense to the first clause — before thorns make your pots ready. The second clause, he admits, remains very difficult. What the poet apparently intends is to compare the sudden overthrow of the wicked, before their arms could succeed, to the disappearance of the fuel before it had time to heat the pot.

C.H. Spurgeon reaches the same sense by staging the scene twice. The pot is put upon the hook to prepare a feast of joy and the fuel placed beneath, but before the thorns are lit a storm comes and sweeps all away, the pot overturned and the fuel scattered. Or the thorns are kindled and the flame is so rapid that the fire is out before any heat is produced, the meat remains raw, and the work is altogether a failure. The malicious wretch puts on his great seething pot and gathers his fuel, meaning to play the cannibal with the godly, but he reckons without the Lord of hosts, and an unexpected tempest removes all trace of him, and his fire, and his feast, and that in a moment.

Adam Clarke reads the same suddenness as a measure of time. From the moment the fire of God’s wrath is kindled about them it will be but a moment before they are entirely consumed — a time so short that it may be likened to the first blaze of dry thorns under a pot, before the heat has penetrated the metal. The whirlwind he identifies with the suffocating simoom, which destroys life in an instant and without warning, so that while they are living and active the whirlwind of God’s wrath sweeps them away. John Wesley agrees that they are taken violently and while alive, as Korah was. John Gill notes that dry thorns give a quick heat, so that the pots soon feel them, and marks the change of mode: from imprecations the psalmist here proceeds to prophesy.
10:
What the righteous rejoice at is guarded carefully. John Gill distinguishes the object of the joy: not the evils and miseries simply considered, nor any private affection, but the glory of divine justice displayed in them and the goodness of God shown in delivering his people; the vengeance is the punishment inflicted by the Lord, to whom vengeance belongs, and since his judgments are sometimes manifest, the righteous observe them. John Wesley gives the same account in a line: they rejoice for the blessed effects of it, the vindication of God’s honour and the deliverance of all good men. Adam Clarke makes it evidential — the righteous man has in it a strong proof of the divine providence, of God’s hatred against sinners and of his continual care of his followers.

The washing of the feet they take as a measure of slaughter. Adam Clarke says the words can only mean that the killing would be so great, and so near the dwelling of the righteous, that he could not go out without dipping his feet in the blood of the wicked; and the Syriac, Latin, Greek, Ethiopic and Arabic, he reports, all read hands instead of feet. John Wesley puts it hypothetically, that there would be so great a slaughter of his enemies that he might, if he pleased, wash his feet in their blood. Charles Ellicott gives the picture in three words: wading deep in blood.

Adam Clarke then does something none of the others do — he disowns the verse. Everything that is vindictive in the psalms, he writes, must be considered as totally alien from the spirit of the gospel, and not at all to be imitated under our dispensation; and if this passage is really vindictive, though he thinks it will admit of the milder interpretation he has given, it is to be considered as not belonging to that state in which the Son of man is come, not to destroy men’s lives but to save.

The closing verse is read as a conclusion drawn by onlookers. John Gill makes the speaker any man and every man, and especially one who is observing, wise and knowing, concluding from such a dispensation of things what follows. Adam Clarke presses the word for reward, which properly means fruit: the righteous man has not sown his seed in vain, nor planted and watered in vain, but has the fruit of his labours and eats the fruit of his doings, while for the wicked it is ill, since the reward of his hands has been given him. And on the last clause he insists that there is a God who does not defer judgment entirely till the judgment-day but executes it now, even in this earth, giving such proof of his hatred to sin that every considerate mind is convinced of it — whence the two maxims, that there is even here a reward for the righteous, and that there is a God who even now judgeth in the earth.

Adam Clarke closes the chapter by returning to the charmers of the fifth verse with evidence of his own. He reports having seen Indian priests who professed to charm not only serpents but the most ferocious wild beasts, even the enraged elephant and the royal tiger; two priests of Budhoo educated under his own care repeated the Sanscrit incantations to him and asserted that they had seen their power repeatedly put to the test, and he regrets having mislaid the words, since it is to charms of this nature that the psalmist most undoubtedly alludes. The Hebrew term rendered charmer, he adds, comes from a verb meaning to join or put together, that is, to string together the unintelligible words or sentences which formed the spell; and he recalls once meeting a man who professed to remove diseases by pronouncing an unintelligible jingling jargon of words oddly tacked together.
